title: Feasibility of running the ET-SoC-1 without its heatsink
description: Whether an ET-SoC-1 card can run with its heatsink off so that a sensor can look straight at the chip, worked out from the cards' measured leakage laws, the fitted heatsink model and Monte Carlo models of the bare package, and checked against vendor θJA tables, published bare-processor runs and infrared-window cooler studies: in the model a bare 600 MHz card almost never holds a stable temperature (1 of 3,600 draws), and a sensor would see a plated lid at nearly one temperature. A slower clock does not rescue it: the lowest the firmware can set, 100 MHz, removes about 7% of the idle power, and even at the firmware's lowest voltages a bare card needs a thermal resistance of about 2.7 °C/W or less, which still air never gives and a fan gives in about a fifth of draws on aifoundry2 and aifoundry3; a 3–6 m/s blower passes under half of cold power-ons in the measurement plan's model. Through a taped lid at 100 MHz, lock-in would show single shires within about 10 s, but a bare card leaves about a minute for it only with a fan and only in some power-ons, behind an automatic power cut and after the measurement plan. The chip's own sensors, heatsink on, are the safe way to see where the work runs: one usable sensor on the stock firmware, a per-shire map only with a rebuilt boot loader. A thermocouple taped to the heatsink base, heatsink on and never between lid and heatsink, is safe with the card off; one soldered into a groove in the lid needs the lab's consent and carries moderate risk.
